title: Repeated Sysmon DNS Queries with Long Labels
exclusions: Reports a local screening heuristic: at least three distinct Sysmon Event ID 22 query names attributed to the same endpoint/process during one completed 15-minute search slice, where each query contains a text label of at least 50 characters. The 50-character label and three-query thresholds are deployment choices—not Microsoft, Splunk, MITRE, or DNS protocol definitions—and require baselining. The rule does not calculate entropy, decode payloads, inspect packet contents/types/TTL, prove tunneling, distinguish command-and-control from exfiltration, establish domain ownership/reputation, or detect short/low-frequency channels. Sysmon reports process DNS API activity whether successful, failed, cached, or not; it is not authoritative resolver traffic and can have unknown process attribution. The detector does not block DNS, terminate processes, isolate endpoints, modify Sysmon, or attest compliance.
evidence: After deployment, retain the qualified Sysmon binary/configuration hash and Event ID 16 changes; effective XML input and Splunk Add-on for Sysmon version; endpoint/source/field health; approved thresholds and baseline analysis; `windows_sysmon_repeated_long_dns_labels` saved-search definition/ACL/schedule/dispatch; every aggregate result plus contributing raw Event ID 22 XML; process, resolver, proxy/network, domain, threat-intelligence, and software/change context; disposition; exact bounded exception; and dated long-label, below-threshold, boundary, unknown-process, cached/failed, duplicate, delayed, extraction-loss, and recovery tests. This documentation-only review generated no DNS traffic, endpoint event, saved search, alert, dashboard, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated index and fixed dispatch slice, replay three authentic-shaped Sysmon EventCode 22 XML records on `dns-test-01` with the same Image and ProcessGuid, distinct QueryName values each containing a 52-character label plus `.example.test`, distinct EventRecordID values, and valid QueryStatus/QueryResults. Expect exactly one aggregate row with `unique_long_queries=3`, `long_query_events=3`, `max_label_length=52`, all three queries, preserved process identity, and `use_case=UC-1.2.121`. Repeat one record with an unknown Image/zero ProcessGuid and verify it remains visible under an explicit unknown attribution bucket.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Replay only two distinct qualifying queries for one process, three queries whose longest label is 49 characters, three qualifying queries split across different ProcessGuid values, EventCode 22 from another source, EventCode 21 from the correct source, and records outside the completed slice; expect zero rows for each case. Replay duplicate copies with the same endpoint/EventRecordID and prove collection health reports the duplicate while notification logic does not inflate the unique-query count. Prove an exact unexpired endpoint/process/domain-suffix exception affects delivery only after base aggregation; expired, wildcard, host-only, or source-health exceptions must not hide evidence.

dataSources: Microsoft Sysmon Event ID 22 (`DNSEvent`) from `Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Sysmon > Operational`, collected in XML to deployment-chosen `index=windows`, `source=XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`. Required fields are `_time`, `_indextime`, `host`/`Computer`, `source`, `sourcetype`, `EventCode`, `QueryName`, `QueryStatus`, `QueryResults`, `Image`, `ProcessGuid`, `ProcessId`, `User` when present, and `EventRecordID`. Sysmon must be configured to include DNS query events. Resolver, DNS-server, EDR, proxy, and packet telemetry are optional corroboration and are not silently mixed into this raw source contract.
app: Splunk Add-on for Sysmon (`Splunk_TA_microsoft_sysmon`, Splunkbase 5709) 5.0.1 supplies the supported Sysmon input, Event ID 22 field extractions, and Network Resolution CIM knowledge for Splunk Platform 9.2+ and Sysmon 15.0. A deployment app supplies the saved search, source-health content, fixtures, dashboard, baseline, and exact exception lookup. No premium app is required for the raw rule.
spl:
index=windows sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog source="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=22 earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m
| eval endpoint=lower(trim(coalesce(Computer,dvc,dest,host))), query_name=lower(trim(coalesce(QueryName,query,""))), process_path=coalesce(Image,process_path,"unknown"), process_guid=coalesce(ProcessGuid,process_guid,"unknown"), process_id=coalesce(ProcessId,process_id,"unknown"), dns_user=coalesce(User,user,"unknown"), query_status=coalesce(QueryStatus,reply_code_id,"unknown"), query_results=coalesce(QueryResults,answer,"unknown"), event_record_id=coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber,"unknown")
| where len(endpoint)>0 AND len(query_name)>0
| eval query_name=rtrim(query_name,"."), dns_label=split(query_name,".")
| mvexpand dns_label
| eval label_length=len(dns_label)
| eventstats max(label_length) as max_label_length values(eval(if(label_length>=50,dns_label,null()))) as long_labels by endpoint event_record_id process_guid query_name _time
| where max_label_length>=50
| dedup endpoint event_record_id process_guid query_name _time
| stats count as long_query_events dc(query_name) as unique_long_queries max(max_label_length) as max_label_length values(long_labels) as long_labels values(query_name) as queries values(query_status) as query_statuses values(query_results) as query_results min(_time) as first_time max(_time) as last_time values(event_record_id) as event_record_ids by endpoint process_path process_guid process_id dns_user
| where unique_long_queries>=3
| eval first_seen=strftime(first_time,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), last_seen=strftime(last_time,"%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), threshold="max_label_length>=50_characters AND unique_long_queries>=3_per_15_minutes", use_case="UC-1.2.121"
| table endpoint process_path process_guid process_id dns_user first_seen last_seen long_query_events unique_long_queries max_label_length long_labels queries query_statuses query_results event_record_ids threshold use_case
| sort 0 -unique_long_queries -max_label_length endpoint process_path
description: Identifies endpoint/process groups that issue at least three distinct Sysmon DNS queries during a completed 15-minute slice when every retained query contains a label 50 or more characters long. Results preserve process identity, counts, maximum label length, queries, statuses/results, event records, exact local threshold, and unknown attribution rather than declaring tunneling.
value: Repeated near-maximum-length DNS labels can carry encoded application data and deserve correlation with process lineage and resolver/network evidence. Process-attributed aggregation accelerates review of possible DNS-based command-and-control or exfiltration while reducing single-query noise and avoiding the unsupported conclusion that a long CDN, security, or service-discovery name is malicious.
implementation: Deploy and qualify Sysmon 15.0 plus Splunk Add-on for Sysmon 5.0.1, include Event ID 22 in the reviewed configuration, collect the Operational channel as XML, and validate QueryName/status/results plus process fields. Save `windows_sysmon_repeated_long_dns_labels`, run every 15 minutes with `earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m`, and trigger when any process has three distinct queries whose maximum label is at least 50 characters. Baseline exact software/domain patterns and investigate with process and resolver/network context before assigning severity.
visualization: Dashboard `Windows — Long DNS Labels`: place expected-endpoint Sysmon/Event-22/source health and unknown-process rates first. Show a 24-hour process timeline, endpoint/process table with unique queries and maximum label length, distribution of label lengths, suffix/software prevalence, query status, and raw XML drilldown. Restrict full query/result visibility where DNS names may contain sensitive identifiers. Never label a row `DNS tunnel confirmed`, and never display missing Event ID 22 coverage as normal query behavior.
cimSpl:
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as first_time max(_time) as last_time from datamodel=Network_Resolution where NOT DNS.record_type IN ("Pointer","PTR","SOA","SRV") by DNS.src DNS.dest DNS.query DNS.record_type DNS.process_path DNS.user
| rename DNS.* as *
| eval query_length=len(query)
| eventstats avg(query_length) as avg_query_length stdev(query_length) as stdev_query_length
| where stdev_query_length>0 AND query_length>(avg_query_length+2*stdev_query_length)
| eval z_score=(query_length-avg_query_length)/stdev_query_length
| table first_time last_time src dest process_path user query record_type count query_length avg_query_length stdev_query_length z_score
| sort 0 -z_score
schema: Native Microsoft Sysmon Event ID 22 XML; optional CIM Network_Resolution
dataModelAcceleration: Optional and semantically separate. Splunk Add-on for Sysmon maps Event ID 22 to Network Resolution, and Splunk Security Content publishes a population-level query-length standard-deviation analytic. Validate raw-to-CIM source, query, process, user, answer, record type, reply code, and timestamp parity plus acceleration lag/range before use. That CIM search compares total query length across its population; it is not equivalent to this raw per-label, per-process, three-query rule and must have its own baseline and tests.

knownFalsePositives:
Rows are genuine repeated long-label DNS observations; the false positive is treating this local heuristic as proof of tunneling.

1. **Endpoint security, EDR, DNS filtering, or certificate-reputation service** — Security clients can encode hashes, device IDs, or reputation keys in long labels. Match exact signed process/hash, product/version, documented vendor suffix, tenant, endpoint role, and expected query format. Suppress only that tuple and review after upgrades.

2. **Cloud/CDN telemetry and content-addressed services** — Browsers, updaters, and collaboration clients may resolve long generated labels. Verify application owner, signer, parent, suffix registration/hosting, prevalence, query success, and network destination. A common domain alone is not sufficient because subdomains can be tenant-controlled.

3. **Microsoft/enterprise service discovery and device enrollment** — Management, activation, enrollment, and identity workflows can generate structured names during onboarding. Correlate provisioning job, device-management check-in, exact process/suffix, target ring, and bounded enrollment window.

4. **Backup, storage, package, or artifact client** — Content hashes and object identifiers can appear in DNS names. Validate package, repository/domain ownership, scheduled job, process lineage, label format, and expected data direction; a signed binary can still be abused.

5. **Authorized DNS security test or red-team tunnel simulation** — Match exercise ID, named operator, exact endpoint/process/domain, exclusive UTC window, expected query pattern, and cleanup. Preserve the base result and alert evidence.

6. **Internationalized/punycode or vendor-generated long names** — Long `xn--` labels or machine-generated identifiers may be legitimate. Confirm user/application workflow, registered suffix, process, recurrence, and owner; do not globally exempt punycode or all 50-character labels.

7. **Unknown process attribution for short-lived programs** — Event ID 22 can contain unknown Image/ProcessGuid in some conditions. Correlate ProcessId/time with Event ID 1 and endpoint telemetry; treat persistent unknown-attribution rate as data quality, not a safe process allow-list.

8. **Duplicate local/WEC collection or replay** — Compare endpoint, channel, EventRecordID, raw hash, and index time. Correct routing/checkpoint overlap. The SPL deduplicates exact record identity for counting, but source health must retain and report duplication.

**Safe notification suppression:** apply `windows_long_dns_label_exceptions.csv` after base aggregation, keyed by exact lowercase endpoint or governed asset group, full process path and preferably hash, registered/specific suffix, expected label-format identifier, numeric `valid_from`/exclusive `valid_until`, owner, approver, ticket, and reason. Reject global suffix wildcards, host-only/process-only entries, open-ended dates, unknown-process exceptions, and exceptions that hide source-health failures. Preserve original aggregate and contributing raw records.
hardware: Windows 8.1 and later endpoints/servers with Microsoft Sysmon 15.0 configured for DNS Event ID 22 and XML collection. Microsoft notes Event ID 22 was added for Windows 8.1. DNS operations bypassing the observed API/path, endpoints without Sysmon, and authoritative resolver/network behavior require separate telemetry.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft Sysmon Event ID 22 documentation, RFC 1035 DNS limits, current Splunk Sysmon add-on/CIM and Security Content documentation, and MITRE ATT&CK DNS behavior; no Sysmon configuration, DNS query, packet/resolver comparison, SPL/CIM execution, threshold baseline, fixture replay, exception, alert, dashboard, privacy review, or Microsoft/Splunk/DNS/endpoint-security SME runtime sign-off

cost.search_load_notes: The 15-minute raw search expands DNS labels before reducing to EventRecordID and process groups. Work scales with Event ID 22 volume and labels per query; constrain the exact source/time and measure `mvexpand` memory. Optional high-cardinality CIM query summarization adds shared acceleration cost.
sources: Microsoft Sysmon Operational XML Event ID 22

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and heuristic contract

Assign endpoint-security, Sysmon configuration, DNS/network, Splunk collection/content, privacy, threat-intelligence, software-owner, and incident-response roles. Inventory in-scope Windows endpoints, direct versus WEF/WEC routes, endpoint roles, Sysmon configuration/version, DNS software, expected high-volume/long-label applications, and data-retention restrictions. Install Microsoft Sysmon 15.0 and Splunk Add-on for Sysmon 5.0.1 through controlled deployment; qualify Windows, Sysmon, forwarder, add-on, CIM, indexer, search-head, and Splunk Cloud versions.

Microsoft says Event ID 22 is generated when a process executes a DNS query whether it succeeds or fails and whether cached or not. Therefore it is process-side API telemetry, not packet or authoritative resolver evidence. The payload normally supplies QueryName, QueryStatus, QueryResults, Image, ProcessGuid, and ProcessId, but short-lived-process attribution can be unknown and record-type/TTL semantics are not guaranteed by the raw event. Preserve those limitations.

RFC 1035 limits a DNS wire-format label to 63 octets. This SPL counts characters in Sysmon's displayed name and uses 50 characters merely as a near-limit screening point; it is not protocol validation and differs for non-ASCII representation. Three distinct qualifying names per process in 15 minutes is also a local noise-control threshold. Baseline and tune both while retaining a versioned threshold rationale.

## Step 1 — Configure and verify Event ID 22 collection

Merge a reviewed `DnsQuery` include into the organization's Sysmon configuration. Avoid copying broad community exclusions that remove browsers, security agents, or common suffixes before their risk is understood. Record the active config hash, verify Event ID 16 after changes, and inspect Event ID 255 errors. Confirm **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > Sysmon > Operational** locally.

Collect XML through an app-owned input:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational]
disabled = 0
renderXml = true
index = windows
checkpointInterval = 5
```

The add-on documents `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` and source `XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational`. Do not edit `default`. For WEF/WEC, use dedicated collector guidance, preserve originating Computer as endpoint, measure subscription latency, and prevent direct plus collector duplication. DNS names/results can contain internal hosts, tenant identifiers, or encoded data, so restrict raw fields and exports.

For representative browser, service, command-line, successful, failed, and cached queries, compare Event Viewer XML with Splunk. Verify QueryName, QueryStatus, QueryResults, Image, ProcessGuid, ProcessId, User where supplied, EventRecordID, provider, channel, event version, event time, and index time. Correlate ProcessGuid to Event ID 1. Record cases where Sysmon reports unknown Image/zero GUID; do not replace them with guessed process names.

## Step 2 — Establish source health independently

Maintain expected endpoint/config/route/owner inventory. Health searches must detect no recurring Sysmon telemetry, no Event ID 22 where test/normal workloads establish expectation, Event ID 16 drift, Event ID 255 errors, wrong source/type/provider/channel, missing QueryName or EventRecordID, unknown Image/GUID rate, indexing delay, clock skew, duplicate routes/record IDs, and add-on extraction drift. Event ID 22 volume can legitimately vary, so combine deployment/service/config telemetry with controlled canaries where permitted.

Separate data quality from the security finding. No rows can mean no qualifying behavior, no DNS events, aggressive endpoint filtering, unsupported Windows, or broken collection. Dashboard coverage must show that ambiguity. Compare endpoint events with resolver telemetry on sampled systems to understand caches, local names, encrypted DNS/proxy paths, and visibility gaps; do not expect one-to-one counts without documenting semantics.

## Step 3 — Save and understand the search

Save the sidecar SPL as `windows_sysmon_repeated_long_dns_labels`. Schedule every 15 minutes with `earliest=-20m@m latest=-5m@m`, evaluating one complete 15-minute slice after a fixed five-minute ingestion allowance. Measure p99 direct/WEC delay; adjust schedule and controls together if needed. Trigger when result count is greater than zero and group delivery by endpoint/process GUID plus a bounded time window.

The base clause fixes the deployment index, XML source type, exact Sysmon channel, EventCode 22, and closed window. Normalization preserves QueryStatus/Results and makes missing process/user/record fields explicit. A trailing root dot is removed only for label splitting. `mvexpand` creates one row per displayed label; `eventstats` restores the event's maximum and qualifying labels. The first `where` keeps events with a 50-character label. Exact event identity is deduplicated before process aggregation so a duplicated collector record does not inflate count. `dc(query_name)` enforces three distinct names, not three copies.

Measure `mvexpand` memory and result limits at production volume. If required, implement an equivalent tested `mvmap`/custom function or precomputed field; do not silently truncate. ProcessGuid is the primary grouping context, with path/PID retained. Unknown GUIDs may aggregate by endpoint/path and must be labelled as lower-confidence attribution rather than suppressed.

Do not claim NXDOMAIN or DGA detection: QueryStatus needs version-specific interpretation and Sysmon does not provide authoritative resolver response analytics here. Do not calculate `dc(QueryName)>100` only after filtering long names and then describe it as all-process DNS volume. The old conjunction made its stated OR thresholds misleading. Do not call a 50-character label “high entropy”; entropy requires a separate algorithm and baseline.

## Step 4 — Validate thresholds and source semantics

Use authentic-shaped XML from the qualified Sysmon/add-on pair and fixed dispatch times. Execute both control scenarios. Add cases for label lengths 49, 50, 63, total long name with short labels, trailing dot, uppercase normalization, repeated same name, three distinct names, split process GUIDs, unknown process, Unicode/punycode, empty status/results, failed and cached queries, multiple answers, EventRecordID missing, and queries exactly at earliest/latest boundaries. Assert field shape after `mvexpand`, dedup, and stats.

Generate safe lab traffic only to domains owned/reserved for testing, using an approved resolver and disposable endpoint. Do not query unowned tunnel infrastructure or embed sensitive data. Compare Event Viewer, raw Splunk XML, endpoint process creation, resolver logs, packet/network sensor where approved, and expected query names. Verify that cached versus wire behavior can differ while Sysmon still records the process query.

Replay direct/WEC duplicates, delayed events, checkpoint reset, clock skew, large result values, and high-cardinality process/query sets. Test optional Network_Resolution normalization/acceleration separately against the published Splunk Security Content standard-deviation analytic; do not claim equivalence. Test exact exceptions, expiry, malformed rows, changed process/suffix, evidence retention, and continued source-health alerts. Keep draft until thresholds, source health, privacy, fixtures, alert, dashboard, exceptions, and response are accepted.

## Step 5 — Investigate and respond

Alert text should say `Repeated long DNS labels observed from <process> on <endpoint>`, not `DNS tunnel`. Include window, counts, maximum label length, full queries under access control, status/results, process path/GUID/PID/user, endpoint role, baseline/prevalence, source health, exception, and runbook.

Responder sequence:
1. Verify exact source/EventCode, raw XML, record IDs, process attribution quality, event/index times, and duplicate route state.
2. Correlate ProcessGuid with Event ID 1, parent/command line, signer/hash, user/logon, file provenance, EDR, service/task, and software inventory.
3. Parse registered suffix/subdomain structure; assess label format/entropy only with a validated method. Check domain ownership, age/reputation, passive DNS, prevalence, and approved application documentation.
4. Compare endpoint QueryStatus/Results with recursive-resolver, proxy/DoH policy, firewall, and network-flow/packet evidence. Determine whether queries reached the network and what responses/connections followed.
5. Check frequency over longer periods, bytes/direction where available, regularity, process fleet prevalence, and correlated command-and-control/exfiltration behavior.
6. For authorized software, document exact version/process/suffix/format and add only a bounded exception. For suspicious behavior, follow approved endpoint/network containment and evidence-preservation procedures.
7. Confirm process/domain disposition, source health, no unexpected recurrence, exception expiry, and retained evidence before closure.

Never block a suffix, kill a process, isolate a server, or alter DNS/Sysmon automatically from this heuristic. A broad block can disrupt security, identity, cloud, or business services. Retain DNS names/results under privacy and legal policy; the advisory 90-day value is not a regulatory requirement.

## Step 6 — Troubleshoot product-specific failures

- **No Event ID 22:** verify Windows support, Sysmon service/version, active DnsQuery configuration and Event ID 16, local Operational channel, Event ID 255, input deployment, queues, index, and RBAC.
- **Image/GUID unknown:** preserve the event, correlate PID/time with Event ID 1 and EDR, inspect short-lived-process behavior, and track attribution-quality rate. Never allow-list unknown.
- **QueryName null:** inspect raw XML EventData, event/add-on version, source identity, XML rendering, props/transforms placement, and field aliases.
- **Resolver has a query but Sysmon does not:** clients, services, proxies, kernel paths, DoH, caching, or endpoint filters can differ. This UC is not resolver completeness.
- **Sysmon has a query but resolver does not:** Microsoft says cached queries still generate Event ID 22; also inspect resolver choice and encrypted DNS/proxy paths.
- **Counts inflated:** inspect EventRecordID/raw hash for local plus WEC collection or replay and confirm dedup identity. Repair routing rather than suppressing the process.
- **Long-label security agent floods alerts:** prove exact product/process/hash/suffix/format/owner and use an expiring exception; do not exclude all Program Files, signed binaries, or vendor parent domains.
- **CIM analytic differs:** verify Network_Resolution tags/fields, add-on/CIM versions, source population, acceleration lag/range, summaries-only macro, record types, and total-query versus label-length semantics.
- **Late WEC events missed:** measure `_indextime-_time`, WEC subscription mode, queues, and clocks; resize the fixed delay and test boundaries rather than overlapping unlimited lookbacks.
grandmaExplanation: We look for a program repeatedly asking DNS about names with unusually long pieces. Some normal cloud and security tools do this too, so the team checks the program and network records before calling it harmful.
